reason: The sources provide over 10 cross-verified claims detailing the extreme environment, supermassive black hole flares, and cyclic 500-million-year starburst fireworks at the Milky Way core.
story: Deep at the heart of the Milky Way, roughly 25,000 light-years from Earth, lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole with about 4 million times the mass of our Sun. Thick lanes of interstellar dust block visible light from reaching Earth, but X-ray and radio observatories reveal a realm of cosmic violence. Thousands of stellar-mass black holes and massive Wolf-Rayet stars cluster in the central parsec. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory caught Sagittarius A* erupting in a record-breaking X-ray flare 400 times brighter than its normal state, likely caused by an asteroid torn apart by gravity or tangled magnetic fields in infalling gas. But even bigger fireworks loom. Astronomers Antony Stark and Chris Martin discovered that interstellar gas collecting near the galactic core is reaching critical density. In approximately 200 million years, this gas will trigger a giant starburst, producing supernova explosions every single year in a galactic cycle that repeats every 500 million years.
angle: In 200 million years, gas gathering at the center of the Milky Way will trigger a giant starburst, causing supernovae to detonate every single year.

claims.claim: Sagittarius A* is a supermassive black hole located at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.
Sagittarius A* has an estimated mass of about 4 million solar masses.
NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory detected a record-breaking X-ray flare from Sagittarius A* that was 400 times brighter than normal.
One theoretical cause for the 400-times X-ray flare is an asteroid torn apart by Sagittarius A*'s gravity.
Another theoretical cause for the giant flare is the reconfiguration of tightly packed, tangled magnetic field lines within infalling gas.
Interstellar dust along the line of sight prevents the Galactic Center from being studied at visible light wavelengths.
The Galactic Center is located approximately 25,000 to 26,000 light-years away from Earth.
Astronomers Antony Stark and Chris Martin mapped the gas density in a 400-light-year region around the Galactic Center.
A dense ring of interstellar gas near the Galactic Center is approaching a critical density required for rapid star formation.
The Galactic Center is predicted to experience a major starburst episode in approximately 200 million years.
During the upcoming starburst episode, supernovae will explode at 100 times their current rate, averaging roughly one supernova per year.
The Milky Way undergoes a major starburst episode near its center roughly once every 500 million years.
An estimated population of 20,000 to 25,000 stellar-mass black holes is predicted to settle into the central parsec around Sagittarius A*.
The Galactic Center region contains a notable population of massive, evolved Wolf-Rayet stars.

disputed: Exact mass of Sagittarius A*: S1 lists 3.7 to 4.3 million solar masses, while S2 cites about 4.5 million solar masses. Attribute as 'about 4 million solar masses'.
Exact trigger of the 400-times X-ray flare: S1 and S2 present two competing theories (asteroid tidal disruption vs magnetic reconnection). Script should attribute both as leading hypotheses.
